activities.anchor: choosing the angle that turns a ten-line problem
activities.caption: pair each angle with the integration that buys it
activities.name: mechAngleMatch

config.prompt: One law, three useful angles — pair each with what it does:

pairs.right: integrate over distance — answers "how fast?" without caring about the path
integrate over time — collision questions without the enormous forces inside the impact
turn the whole apparatus sideways — spinning shafts as cleanly as sliding blocks

config.why: They are not different laws: each is Newton's second law re-packaged — by distance, by time, or by axis.

activities.anchor: it is where mistakes are caught
activities.caption: rebuild the free-body procedure
activities.name: mechFbdOrder

config.prompt: The free-body ritual, in order — drag the steps into place:
items: Isolate the one body you care about
Draw every external force acting on it as an arrow
Hunt the gaps: a missing support or a forgotten friction arrow shows on paper
config.why: A gap on paper is visible; a gap inside algebra is invisible — that is the whole point of drawing first.

activities.anchor: One trigonometric decomposition turned a muddy real situation
activities.caption: drop the marker on the lifting share
activities.name: mechSledgePlace

config.prompt: The gardener's 200 N pull is held 30° above the horizontal. Place the marker on the vertical share doing the lifting:
config.why: 200 × sin 30° = 100 N straight up — it lightens the sledge from 392 N to about 292 N pressing on the ground, and the friction falls with it.

activities.anchor: the ground's push acts on you, your push acts on the ground
activities.caption: one line of the third-law note cancels wrongly
activities.name: mechThirdLawSpot

config.prompt: A note on Newton's third law — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: A third-law pair is equal in size and opposite in direction.
The two members act on different bodies — one on you, one on the ground.
Because they are equal and opposite, they cancel and nothing can accelerate.
A sprinter accelerates because only one member of the pair appears in the sprinter's own diagram.
The matching force belongs to the Earth's bookkeeping, and the Earth barely notices.
config.correction: Cancellation requires both forces to act on the same body; a third-law pair never meets that condition, so the sprinter is free to accelerate.
config.why: Action and reaction are a bookkeeping pair across two bodies, not a balance on one.

activities.anchor: where an Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer
activities.caption: true or false — who falls faster?
activities.name: mechFallJudge

statements.s: Without air resistance, every mass accelerates under gravity at the same 9.81 m/s².
statements.why: Mass appears on both sides of F = m·a and cancels.

statements.s: Gravity pulls harder, per kilogram, on the heavier object.
statements.why: Per kilogram the pull is identical — weight and inertia grow together and cancel.

statements.s: A bowling ball beats a falling leaf only because air drag robs the leaf sooner relative to its weight.
statements.why: The race is settled by drag versus weight, not by gravity picking favourites.

statements.s: Doubling a body's mass doubles its free-fall acceleration.
statements.why: Free-fall acceleration stays 9.81 m/s² whatever the mass.

activities.anchor: two short equations do most of the work
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the kinematics that sets braking
activities.name: mechKinCloze

config.text: For steady acceleration, %%0%% grows in proportion to time (v = v₀ + a·t), while distance grows with the %%1%% of time — one reason a car at twice the speed needs far more than twice the road to stop.
config.hint: The same squaring that sets braking distances lives in the second blank.

activities.anchor: why the outer edge of a grinding wheel screams
activities.caption: call the tip speed
activities.name: mechTipEstimate

config.prompt: A large wind-turbine blade turns slowly and serenely at the hub. Roughly what speed can its tip reach in strong winds?
config.why: v = ω·r — modest angular speed times a very large radius: the tip passes 250 km/h while the hub barely seems to move.
config.context: Same law at small scale: the rim of a spinning disc howls while its middle is silent.

activities.anchor: why flywheel designers push mass outward on purpose
activities.caption: which curve is the inertia law?
activities.name: mechInertiaTrace

config.prompt: A fixed mass moved farther from the axis — which curve is its moment of inertia?
config.why: I grows with the square of distance: doubling the mass doubles I, but the same mass at twice the radius quadruples it — which is why light rims can out-muscle a heavy frame.
